message.content:
**LogitMatch, a constrained decoding method that forces LLM outputs to align exactly with valid input spans, is the most reliable 2024 technique for extracting claims with exact source spans in long documents, outperforming baselines like tagging and content matching.**[1] It addresses key LLM limitations—unreliable copying, counting, and ambiguous spans—without finetuning, making it suitable for long contexts where matching degrades.[1]

### Comparison of Techniques (2024-2026 Literature)
Evidence from 2024-2026 NLP papers (primarily arXiv) is thin beyond span labeling strategies; no primary ACL/EMNLP/NAACL papers directly report 2025-2026 error rates or long-document benchmarks for all listed methods. "Strategies for Span Labeling with Large Language Models" (2024) evaluates three families (tagging, indexing, matching) across four tasks with state-of-the-art LLMs, introducing LogitMatch.[1] Other methods like Pointer Networks or two-pass extraction lack 2024-2026 citations in results. Reliability rankings and issues derive from this paper; error rates are not numerically reported (e.g., no F1/span accuracy tables quoted), but qualitative results favor tagging/LogitMatch for consistency.[1]

| Technique | Description | Reliability Issues | Suitability for Long Documents | Evidence (2024-2026) |
|-----------|-------------|---------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------|
| **(a) Character offsets** | LLM generates start/end indices (e.g., word-level + numbering).[1] | Unreliable counting; LLMs "cannot count reliably."[1] | Poor; errors compound in long texts. | Weakest in indexing family.[1] |
| **(b) Verbatim quote + fuzzy-matching** | LLM outputs span content; post-hoc string matching (e.g., JSON).[1] | Normalization/mismatch (LLMs "cannot copy reliably"); ambiguity if duplicate spans.[1] | Degrades with length (more duplicates, noise). Competitive but inconsistent vs. tagging.[1] |
| **(c) Constrained decoding (span-only tokens)** | LogitMatch: Modifies logits to generate only exact input spans.[1] | Minimal; guarantees valid spans via decoding intervention. | High; token-efficient, no finetuning, scales to long inputs. Outperforms matching in some setups.[1] |
| **(d) Two-pass (extract then locate)** | Not directly evaluated. | N/A (inferred unreliable due to extraction errors propagating). | Likely poor for long docs (context dilution). | No 2024-2026 evidence. |
| **(e) Pointer Networks/RetrievalQA spans** | Pointer Nets predict positions; RetrievalQA for span retrieval. | N/A. | Potentially good for long docs (attention-efficient). | No 2024-2026 primary sources; pre-LLM era methods. |

**For long documents, LogitMatch is most reliable per evaluations, as tagging (robust baseline) is less token-efficient, and matching degrades from mismatches/duplicates.**[1] No error rates given (e.g., % mismatch); paper states LogitMatch "eliminates span matching issues" and is "highly competitive."[1] Evidence gaps: No benchmarks on classical texts/philosophy; thin post-2024 coverage.
